question: A 2-year-old child with severe respiratory distress has a respiratory rate of 6/min and decreasing oxygen saturation despite high-flow oxygen. You initiate bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation. Which of the following is the MOST important technical element to ensure effective BVM ventilation in a young child?

answers.text: Using an adult-sized bag to deliver adequate tidal volume

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An adult-sized bag risks over-inflation (barotrauma) in a small child. Paediatric BVM bags (250–500 mL for infants/small children) should be used, and breaths should only be enough to produce visible chest rise.

answers.text: Achieving a complete mask seal using the EC-clamp technique, with head in neutral or slight sniff position

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Effective BVM ventilation depends primarily on a complete face-mask seal. The EC-clamp technique (3 fingers on the mandible, 2 fingers on the mask) achieves this. In infants/young children, the head should be in a neutral or slight sniff position (NOT hyperextended, which can kink the relatively compliant trachea). Squeeze the bag gently to see chest rise — avoid over-inflation.

answers.text: Hyperextending the neck to maximally open the airway before bagging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hyperextension is appropriate for adults/older children but should be AVOIDED in infants and young children. Their airway is compliant and hyperextension can kink the trachea. Use a neutral or slight sniff position for infants and young children.

answers.text: Delivering breaths at the child's spontaneous respiratory rate to synchronise with breathing efforts

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When a child requires BVM ventilation, their spontaneous effort is typically inadequate. Breaths should be delivered at the appropriate rate for age (approximately 12–20/min for children), timed to produce visible chest rise. Synchronisation with an inadequate effort does not ensure adequate ventilation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Effective BVM ventilation in a child depends on: (1) correct head position (neutral/sniff, NOT hyperextended in infants), (2) a complete mask seal using the EC-clamp technique, and (3) gentle bag squeeze to achieve visible chest rise only.

Correct. A good mask seal with the EC-clamp technique and appropriate head position is the foundation of effective BVM ventilation. Deliver breaths until visible chest rise is seen — do not over-inflate.
